title: Fostering inclusion to strengthen the US STEM enterprise
content: It is hard to escape the news regarding DEI issues, so we thought we would take a moment to once again discuss how DEI is not only not antagonistic but also contributes a resounding net positive to the prosperity of the United States and to societies elsewhere. We are stimulated to write this brief commentary by the publication in this issue of the Education article, “Students express minimal resistance to inclusive biology activities highlighting the diversity of scientists” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag029), by Costello and colleagues. Their article provides a comprehensive data set demonstrating that discussing the diversity of scientists in the classroom is met with no student resistance. Given that DEI programs offer the opportunity to recruit underrepresented groups to STEM fields, it is very low-hanging fruit to align STEM with DEI initiatives to strengthen the scientific endeavor in the United States and elsewhere. Underrepresented means just that, just like an underserved market, or an underexploited resource, underrepresented groups are where we should especially recruit because we have a shortage of STEM personnel. Other countries are exploiting our STEM community, and so we should “exploit” an underrecruited population. And, as the Costello and colleagues’ article indicates, discussing these issues in the classroom is neutral to those groups that are already well represented in STEM.
